The title of **president of King’s College** was created in 1754 by the original [royal charter](/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") for the university, issued by [George II](/wiki/George_II_of_Great_Britain "George II of Great Britain"), and the power to appoint the president was given to [an autonomous board of trustees](/wiki/Trustees_of_Columbia_University_in_the_City_of_New_York "Trustees of Columbia University in the City of New York"). The university suspended operations upon the outbreak of the [American Revolutionary War](/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"), during which no individual served as president. When it was resuscitated by the [New York State Legislature](/wiki/New_York_State_Legislature "New York State Legislature"), the university was placed directly under the control of the [Board of Regents of the University of the State of New York](/wiki/Board_of_Regents_of_the_University_of_the_State_of_New_York "Board of Regents of the University of the State of New York"); its chancellor, [George Clinton](/wiki/George_Clinton_(vice_president) "George Clinton (vice president)"), served as the *de facto* president of Columbia University.[[1]](

Austerlitz and the preceding campaign profoundly altered the nature of European politics. In three months, the French had occupied Vienna, decimated two armies, and humbled the Austrian Empire. These events sharply contrast with the rigid power structures of the 18th century, when no major European capital was ever held by an enemy army. France and Austria signed a truce on 4 December and the [Treaty of Pressburg](/wiki/Treaty_of_Pressburg_(1805) "Treaty of Pressburg (1805)") 22 days later took the latter out of the war.
